clue.text: Snacks for instance served on Greek island

indicators.note: served on tells you one piece is attached to the other, here coming straight after it

parts.note: Samos is a Greek island in the eastern Aegean
as can mean for instance: 'some animals, as the fox, hunt at night'

explanation.surface: Light bites, say, dished up to holidaymakers on an Aegean isle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served on' attaches AS, in its sense of 'for instance', to the island of SAMOS.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: these fried triangular Indian pastries are a familiar kind of light bite.

clue.text: Harpist using a different instrument

indicators.note: different says the letters of the three words before it are put into another order

parts.note: taken as written, the thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A harp player has switched to playing something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges HARPIST USING A. Only the last word defines, though the whole clue paints a musician changing what they play.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the classical nylon-strung six-string is one kind of musical device for playing.

clue.text: Concerned with single tot being brought up rather spoilt

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means the whole run of pieces is read from bottom to top

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as in a memo heading
I is the Roman numeral one, a single
a tot is a small measure of spirits, a dram

explanation.surface: Worrying about one little child who is being raised somewhat overindulged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being brought up' reads RE + I + DRAM (REIDRAM) upwards. Mardy is northern English dialect for sulky or petulant, so its comparative is 'rather spoilt'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mardy is British dialect for sulky or petulant like a pampered child; this comparative form means somewhat more so.

clue.text: Given position wearing formal attire? That's non-U

indicators.note: non-U, normally shorthand for not upper-class, here literally says that one letter is absent

parts.note: someone suited is dressed in a suit

explanation.surface: Someone handed a post while in a dinner jacket is told that is rather common.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's non-U' takes the U out of SUITED. Non-U is British shorthand for not upper-class in speech or manners, which is how the surface wants it read.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something placed or located in a particular spot has been given its place.

clue.text: Shamefaced female joining male, about to drink up

indicators.note: joining places one piece directly next to the other

parts.note: she is the pronoun for a female

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the assembled piece is read from bottom to top
about means around, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a male
to sip is to drink in small mouthfuls

explanation.surface: An embarrassed woman meets a man who is on the point of finishing his glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' looks like one phrase but splits: 'about' wraps the male round the drink, 'up' turns the result into EPISH, and 'joining' sets that after the female.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both describe someone looking embarrassed or ashamed of themselves.

clue.text: Hound: animal pursuing deer no end

indicators.note: pursuing means the animal comes after the other piece
no end says the final letter of the word before it is dropped

parts.note: a hart is a male deer, especially a red deer stag
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: A hunting dog, a creature that chases deer tirelessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hound' reads as the dog but is a verb here. 'no end' shortens the deer to HAR and 'pursuing' sets the donkey after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: as a verb, to hound someone is to pester or persecute them persistently.

clue.text: Abode accommodating British guy

indicators.note: accommodating means the first word makes room within itself for the other piece

parts.note: an abode is a home

explanation.surface: A residence that is putting up a chap from Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish word for man, used informally in American English for a fellow or chap.

clue.text: Carpet material delivered — there's piece for fitting inside

parts.note: rep is a corded fabric used in upholstery

indicators.note: for fitting inside says the piece is to be placed within the word just before it

parts.note: to rid someone of a burden is to deliver or free them from it
a man is a piece in chess or draughts

explanation.surface: The flooring has arrived, with one section still to be laid indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet material' looks like one phrase but splits: carpet is British slang for telling someone off. 'for fitting inside' places the chess piece within the word for delivered.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, to carpet someone is to tell them off severely, to rebuke them.

clue.text: Garment made of gold oddly included in collection

indicators.note: included in says the pieces before it sit within the word that follows

parts.note: a set is a collection of matching things
in can mean made of, as in a ring in silver

indicators.note: oddly picks the odd-numbered letters of the word before it

explanation.surface: An item of clothing woven from gold thread is, curiously, part of a museum's holdings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made of' is no link word but a piece of the wordplay. 'oddly' takes G and L, and 'included in' puts the four letters INGL within the collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: in British usage this is a sleeveless vest or athletics top, an item of clothing.

clue.text: Current broadcasts about American president finally being inaugurated

indicators.note: being inaugurated means ushered in, so the letter is admitted into the run of other pieces

parts.note: a station airs or broadcasts a programme
re means about or concerning

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Today's news programmes cover a US leader being sworn in at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' poses as an adjective meaning up to date but is the noun. 'finally' gives T, which 'being inaugurated' admits among the other pieces, straight after the broadcasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a flow of wind high in the atmosphere is one kind of moving flow.

clue.text: Very good joke circulated — a beauty?

parts.note: pi is old slang, short for pious, for someone very good or sanctimonious

indicators.note: circulated means sent round, so the word for joke is turned to run the other way

parts.note: a pun is a joke that plays on words

explanation.surface: An excellent gag did the rounds, and it was a cracker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circulated' turns PUN into NUP. PI, short for pious, is a crossword regular for 'very good'.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture of an attractive person put on a wall, or that glamorous person themselves.

clue.text: Lay out twice for car park

parts.note: to lay out money is to spend it
twice says the phrase is read in two senses, one and then the other, which supplies the joining word between them
to lay out goods is to arrange them for show

explanation.surface: Mark out the bays a second time for the parking area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay out' is read two ways, spend and exhibit, and 'twice' joins them with AND. In this British car park you buy a ticket from a machine and leave it showing on the dashboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A British parking area where you buy a ticket from a machine and leave it visible in the windscreen.

clue.text: I struggled, overcome by climber

parts.note: to vie is to struggle or compete against others

explanation.surface: I fought hard but was beaten by a mountaineer.
explanation.walkthrough: The climber is a plant, not a mountaineer: the definition is the whimsical 'overcome by climber'.
explanation.definitionFit: Whimsical description: a wall overgrown with ivy, a climbing plant, has been taken over by it.

clue.text: Showing bias thus? Not entirely

definitions.meaning: to act with partiality, favouring one side, is to behave in this manner
in part, to a limited degree only

explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means both in a biased, one-sided manner and only in part, incompletely.

clue.text: Firm not exactly quiet, finding money

parts.note: firm means solid, hard to the touch
ca is short for circa, Latin for approximately
sh is what you say to ask for quiet

explanation.surface: A company that is far from silent discovers some funds.
explanation.definitionFit: Notes and coins, as opposed to cheques or credit, are funds in their most tangible form.

clue.text: Certain study is required during a French course

indicators.note: is required during says the study must be placed within the span of the other word

parts.note: confit, meat such as duck cooked slowly in its own fat, is a dish of French cuisine
a den is a private room for work, a study

explanation.surface: Some homework is definitely needed while taking a language class.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'French course' is a dish, not a language class, and 'study' is a room, not the verb. 'is required during' puts the room within the dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to be sure of something is to have no doubt about it.

clue.text: Keep desiring woman of easy virtue

parts.note: to desire is to want
on after a verb means continuing, as in walk on or play on, which gives the sense of keep

explanation.surface: Carry on lusting after a lady with loose morals.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'walk on' is to keep walking, so by whimsical analogy to WANT ON is to keep desiring.
explanation.definitionFit: As a dated noun, the word means a promiscuous or immoral person, especially a female one.

clue.text: Don't touch presents belonging to female

parts.note: as a verb, someone presents or hands a prize to the winner
of shows possession, as in the house of the mayor

explanation.surface: Leave alone the gifts that are hers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'presents' looks like gifts but is the verb: one who presents a prize hands it over.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: said as a command, it tells someone to leave something alone.

clue.text: Rise you plan, drastically cut

indicators.note: cut says the three words before it are trimmed at both ends, leaving a run of letters from their middle

explanation.surface: The pay increase you have in mind has been slashed severely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' trims 'you plan, drastically' at both ends, leaving the letters that run from the end of 'you' into the start of 'drastically'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch of high or hilly ground is an elevation in the landscape.

clue.text: Treated allergy, to a great extent

indicators.note: treated means processed or worked on, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A hay-fever sufferer has been given medicine with considerable success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treated' rearranges ALLERGY; the surface makes it sound like a medical report.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both mean mostly or for the most part.

clue.text: Instructed fellow taken on night out

parts.note: a fellow is a man
someone you dated is someone you took out for an evening

explanation.surface: A chap being trained was treated to an evening on the town.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to give someone an official order or commission to act is to direct them.

clue.text: I want kinks on metal objects

indicators.note: kinks are twists, so the two words before it are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the five letters to rearrange
re means on the subject of, concerning

explanation.surface: Someone confesses a fetish involving items of metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kinks' twists I WANT into TINWA; 'on' then gives RE, in its sense of concerning, rather than being a position word.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: pots, pans and plates made of tinplate are household items of this material.

clue.text: Tourist leaves one rupee: he's happy with the service?

indicators.note: leaves means departs, so the rupee goes away from the tourist

parts.note: a tripper is someone on a pleasure outing, a British word for a tourist
R is the abbreviation for rupee, and one says only a single R goes

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker puts down a single rupee coin, pleased with how he was looked after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' looks transitive, the tourist leaving a coin, but here one R departs from TRIPPER, a British word for a day tourist.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who leaves a gratuity for a waiter is showing satisfaction with how they were looked after.

clue.text: Dog's lead put on tailless canine I force inside, trembling?

indicators.note: put on means added to, so the single letter is attached to the shortened word
inside says the two letters just named are placed within what has been built so far
tailless means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a terrier is a small breed of dog, a canine
F is the physics abbreviation for force

indicators.note: lead means the leading, first letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A leash is clipped to a dog with a docked tail, which I shove indoors while it shakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' cuts TERRIER to TERRIE, 'put on' adds the D that 'lead' takes from Dog's, and 'inside' slots IF in.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone very frightened may well be shaking with fear, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Every so often, cook needs ice-cream containers

indicators.note: every so often means at regular intervals, so alternate letters of the two words that follow are taken

explanation.surface: Now and then a chef requires tubs for the ice cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every so often' takes every other letter of 'cook needs', counting straight through both words.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: these wafer holders are what a scoop of the frozen dessert is commonly served in.

clue.text: Container for fish caught with angler's equipment

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
a reel is the winding device on a fishing rod

explanation.surface: A basket holds the fish landed using a fisherman's tackle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' is not about landing fish: it is the cricket scorecard abbreviation C.
explanation.definitionFit: A wicker basket that anglers use to carry their catch.

clue.text: Former official's about-turn before end of case

indicators.note: before says the turned word precedes the single letter
about means round the other way, so the word for turn is read backwards

parts.note: to veer is to turn or change direction

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the word after it

explanation.surface: A retired officer's complete change of mind just as a lawsuit was finishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about-turn' is one word on the surface but two jobs: 'about' reads the word for turn backwards, then 'before' and 'end of' add the last letter of case.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval English local magistrate or steward, a post that no longer exists.

clue.text: Awfully lonely chap with no yen for communication

indicators.note: awfully means badly, so the letters that follow are put in a different order
with no says the yen's letter is left out of the two words

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange once one is removed
Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: A terribly isolated man who has no desire to talk to anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' takes Y out of LONELY CHAP, leaving LONELCHAP for 'Awfully' to rearrange. Yen reads as a longing but is the currency.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: ringing someone up is one way of getting in touch.

clue.text: Axes and mostly flinty tool for scraping

parts.note: X and Y are the two axes of a graph

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter of the word is used

parts.note: flinty means hard and unyielding, stern

explanation.surface: Choppers and a largely stone implement used on hides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axes' is the plural of axis, not of axe: the X and Y of a graph. 'mostly' drops the N of STERN.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon's instrument used to scrape bone.

clue.text: Deceptively cunning, to take in a London school

indicators.note: to take in means to swallow, so the first word goes round the letters that follow

parts.note: fly is British slang for sharp and knowing
LSE is the London School of Economics, a university in London

explanation.surface: Sly in a misleading way, managing to fool a college in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to take in' reads as to fool, but here the British slang word for knowing swallows the article and the college's initials.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both adverbs describe doing something in an untrue, misleading way.
